passages.text: The rope snapped at twenty past three. Haruki heard it before he felt it — a sound like a ruler twanged against a desk, sharp and almost playful, followed by the sudden absence of tension in his harness and the sickening knowledge that he was no longer attached to anything at all. The quarry wall rushed past his face. He grabbed at the rock and felt his fingers scrape across limestone, catching nothing, the stone peeling skin from his knuckles in a single clean stroke. Then his second line caught. The jolt drove the harness into his ribs and stopped the world. He hung there, spinning slowly, fifteen metres above the flooded quarry floor where the water was the colour of mouthwash and just as still. His breathing came in sharp, shallow pulls. Above him, someone was shouting his name. Below him, his reflection stared up from the surface, swinging gently, entirely calm.
passages.label: Opening — Drop (In Medias Res, Quarry)

passages.text: Nell planted the apple tree the autumn her daughter was born. It was a small thing then — barely taller than the spade she’d used to dig the hole, its trunk no thicker than a broom handle, its roots wrapped in damp newspaper like a gift she was giving to the future. Now, sixteen years later, she stood beneath it and couldn’t see the sky. The branches had claimed the corner of the garden entirely, spreading outward with the quiet authority of something that knows it belongs. Apples hung in clusters, green shading to red, warm on one side from the September sun and cool on the other. Nell reached up and twisted one free. It came away with a sound like a full stop: definitive, clean. She held it in her palm and thought about how her daughter no longer fitted in the crook of her arm, how the tree no longer fitted in a pot, how neither of them needed her the way they once had.
passages.label: Opening — Shift (Time Jump, Orchard)

passages.text: From the upper deck, the whole estuary was visible. The two coastlines reached towards each other across a mile of grey-green water, joined by nothing but the ferry’s slow diagonal and the gulls that drifted between them. Jonas leaned on the rail. At this distance, the far shore was a smudge of rooftops and a church spire and the dark line of the coast road. The wind carried the smell of open water — salt and weed and the faint diesel trail of the engine below. He lowered his eyes. The wake spread behind the boat in a wide, foaming V that flattened as it reached the edges, dissolving into the estuary’s own slow current. He looked closer still. At the rail itself, the paint was peeling in small, deliberate curls, each one lifted by years of salt air, and beneath the white was a layer of blue, and beneath that a layer of red, each colour a different year, a different crossing, a different version of the same boat making the same journey.
passages.label: Opening — Zoom (Wide to Close-Up, Ferry Crossing)

passages.text: She found the twenty-pence piece in the car park at Watford Gap services, face-down in a puddle of diesel-sheened rainwater. Bea picked it up, rubbed it on her jeans, and slipped it into her coat pocket without thinking. That was half past four on a Tuesday in February. Inside, the services smelled of floor cleaner and fried food and the particular exhaustion of people who are neither where they came from nor where they’re going. She bought a coffee from a machine that took forty-five seconds and gave her something that tasted of nothing. She sat by the window and watched the lorries come and go, their headlights sweeping across the car park in slow arcs. The table was sticky. The chair was bolted to the floor. A child at the next table dropped a chip and cried as though something irreplaceable had been lost. Bea drank the coffee. She checked her phone. She stood, pushed through the heavy glass doors, and walked back to the car park. The twenty-pence piece was still in her pocket. She set it down on the wet tarmac, face-up this time, and drove away.
passages.label: Full Structure — Link (Ending Mirrors Opening, Motorway Services)

passages.text: The builders had started the cathedral in 1093. Gil knew this because it was carved into a stone by the west door, the numbers worn smooth by nine hundred years of rain and the idle fingers of tourists. He stood in the nave and tilted his head back. The ceiling was so high it seemed to have its own weather — a faint grey haze hung in the upper arches where the cold air met the warmth of the radiators below. Candles burned in a side chapel, their flames perfectly still, each one lit for someone who was missed. He walked closer. The nearest candle had a handwritten label beside it: For Dad. Two words, in biro, on a scrap of paper the size of a bus ticket. The ink had blurred where a thumb had pressed too hard. He stood there for a long time, looking at those two words, and the whole vast building — its pillars, its arches, its nine centuries of stone — contracted to the size of a single flame and a scrap of paper and somebody’s grief.
passages.label: Full Structure — Shift and Zoom Combined (Cathedral)

steps: Plan your structure before writing — decide which moves you will use and where
Open with a Drop: start mid-action or mid-thought, not with 'One day...'
Include at least one Shift — jump forward in time, change perspective, or switch focus
Use a Zoom to move between a wide establishing shot and a close-up sensory detail
End with a Link — echo an image, phrase, or idea from your opening to create a circular shape
method_card.title: Drop, Shift, Zoom, Link
method_card.content: Four structural moves give your writing a clear, purposeful shape. Drop the reader into the middle of the action. Shift time, focus, or perspective. Zoom from wide shot to close-up (or vice versa). Link your ending back to your opening for a satisfying finish.

gold.context: A good response creates a clear structural frame — the opening and ending are connected by a repeated element (an object, a phrase, an image, an action) but the meaning or context has shifted. The middle section should contain enough development that the return feels earned, not forced. The writing should use precise vocabulary, sensory detail, and at least one moment of figurative language. The link should feel satisfying and purposeful — the reader should understand why the writer has circled back.
gold.question: Write a short narrative (any setting, any character) that uses the Link technique. Your ending must echo, mirror, or reverse your opening — a repeated object, phrase, action, or image that returns with changed meaning. The reader should feel the link between the first sentence and the last.

gold.context: A good response narrows focus smoothly and deliberately from panoramic to close-up. Each sentence should bring the reader closer. The final detail should be small but emotionally charged — something that makes the reader feel the significance of the whole scene. The transition from wide to narrow should feel natural (it can use explicit signals like 'he stepped closer' or can narrow simply through the sequence of observations).
gold.question: Write your own Zoom passage — start with the widest possible view of a place and narrow the focus across four or five sentences until you reach one tiny, emotionally significant detail. The final detail should carry the weight of the whole piece.

gold.context: A good Drop opening starts with action, sensation, or a dramatic detail — not background, not 'One day...' or 'It all started when...' The reader should feel as though they have arrived mid-scene. Precise physical details should anchor the moment. The writing should raise questions (What happened? Who is this? Why?) without answering them. At least one sensory detail should place the reader in the scene immediately.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: Notice how the very first sentence drops us into a crisis: "The rope snapped at twenty past three." There's no build-up, no introduction, no 'One sunny morning, Haruki decided to go climbing.' The reader is thrown into the moment of danger immediately. This is a Drop opening.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: Look at what the writer does NOT include. There's no backstory yet — we don't know why Haruki is climbing, who he is, or where the quarry is. All of that can come later. The Drop prioritises the moment over the context, trusting that the reader will keep reading to find out the rest.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: Notice the sensory layering after the Drop. The writer slows time right after the crisis: he "heard it before he felt it", then describes the sound ("like a ruler twanged against a desk"), then the physical sensation ("the sudden absence of tension"), then the thought ("the sickening knowledge"). The Drop gets the reader's attention; the slow-motion detail keeps it.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.content: To write your own Drop opening, find the most dramatic or tense moment in your scene and start there. Write your first sentence as a short, punchy statement of fact. Then slow down and unfold the moment using senses and detail. The rule is: hook first, explain later.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: A Drop opening starts at the point of highest tension: 'The rope snapped at twenty past three.' This seven-word sentence creates instant urgency — the reader needs to know what happens next. The writer then slows time, layering sound ('like a ruler twanged against a desk'), sensation ('the sudden absence of tension'), and thought ('the sickening knowledge') to stretch one second across several lines. To use this structure yourself: start with a short, dramatic first sentence, then expand the moment using sensory detail. Never begin with backstory — drop the reader into the action and let them catch up.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: Identify the camera position. The passage starts with the widest possible shot: "the whole estuary was visible." We see two coastlines, a mile of water, the ferry's path, the gulls. This is the establishing shot — it tells us where we are and what the world looks like from a distance.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: Track the zoom. The passage moves from panoramic (the whole estuary) to medium (Jonas leaning on the rail) to distant detail (the far shore as "a smudge of rooftops and a church spire"). If you read the full passage, the writer continues zooming: to the wake behind the boat, to the rail itself, to the paint peeling in curls — each sentence narrows the focus.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: Consider why this structure works. Moving from wide to close-up creates a natural sense of discovery — the reader feels like they're arriving in the scene, settling in, noticing more as they look more closely. It also controls pacing: wide shots feel calm and expansive, close-ups feel intimate and detailed.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.content: To apply this in your own writing, plan your zoom in three stages: wide (the whole setting), medium (your character in the setting), close (one tiny detail that carries meaning). The close-up should be the most carefully written — it's where your description lands. In this passage, the peeling paint revealing layers of old colour becomes a metaphor for time passing. That's the power of the Zoom: it starts with a landscape and ends with an idea.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The Zoom structure moves through three levels: wide ('the whole estuary was visible' — the panoramic establishing shot), medium ('Jonas leaned on the rail' — the character placed in the scene), and the beginning of the close-up ('a smudge of rooftops and a church spire' — specific details emerging from the distance). Each stage narrows the reader's focus and increases the level of detail. To structure your own writing this way, open with a sentence that establishes the whole setting, then move your camera steadily inward until you reach one small, significant detail. The final close-up should carry emotional weight — it's not just what you see, but what that detail means.

At this distance, the far shore was a smudge of rooftops and a church spire and the dark line of the coast road.

ai_marking_prompts.creative_writing:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor giving formative feedback on a student's short creative writing (around 80-120 words). This is a practice task — your goal is to encourage and develop.

Assess whether the student:
1. Created a clear ATMOSPHERE or MOOD through their writing choices
2. Used SPECIFIC detail rather than vague generalisations
3. Showed some CRAFT — deliberate vocabulary choices, varied sentences, or figurative language
4. Engaged the reader — does the writing create a picture or feeling?

IMPORTANT: This is short creative writing, not an essay. Reward imagination and voice. A student who writes vividly about a simple scene is doing better than one who uses forced figurative language on every line. Quality over quantity. Be genuinely encouraging — creative writing is personal and students need confidence.

Respond in JSON:
{"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences","improvement":"optional suggestion"}

excellent = vivid, engaging writing with clear atmosphere, specific detail, and deliberate craft. Shows a genuine writer's voice
good = creates some atmosphere or imagery, uses some specific detail, shows effort with vocabulary or technique even if inconsistent
needs_work = very generic or vague, mostly tells rather than shows, little evidence of deliberate craft
not_valid = didn't attempt creative writing, wrote a single sentence, or is completely off-topic
ai_marking_prompts.improve_sentence:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor giving formative feedback on a student's rewritten sentence. The student was shown a weak sentence and asked to improve it by upgrading vocabulary, sentence structure, or technique.

Assess whether the student:
1. Made a genuine IMPROVEMENT — is the rewrite better than the original?
2. Addressed the specific weakness (vague vocabulary, telling not showing, flat structure, clichéd language)
3. Maintained the original MEANING while improving the quality

IMPORTANT: There are many valid ways to improve a sentence. Do NOT penalise creative choices. If the student's version is more vivid, precise, or engaging than the original, that counts as improvement even if it's different from what you'd write. Be encouraging.

Respond in JSON:
{"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences","improvement":"optional suggestion"}

excellent = significantly better than the original, shows flair or originality, addresses the weakness effectively
good = clearly improved on the original, addresses the main weakness even if it could go further
needs_work = barely changed, or changed something but not the main weakness, or introduced new problems

ai_marking_prompts.creative_writing_extended:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor giving formative feedback on a student's extended creative writing (around 150-200+ words). This simulates the Paper 1 Q5 creative writing task worth up to 40 marks.

Assess whether the student:
1. Created a sustained ATMOSPHERE or MOOD — not just one good sentence but a consistent feel throughout
2. Used a range of TECHNIQUES — sensory language, figurative language, varied sentence structures, effective punctuation
3. Showed STRUCTURAL awareness — the piece has shape (a beginning that hooks, development, and an ending that resonates)

IMPORTANT: This is formative practice. Reward ambition even when execution is imperfect. A student who attempts a complex structure and partly succeeds is showing more skill than one who plays it safe. Be encouraging but specific about what would strengthen the piece.

Respond in JSON:
{"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"3-4 sentences","improvement":"specific suggestion"}

excellent = sustained atmosphere, range of techniques used effectively, clear structure, accurate SPaG, distinctive voice. This is writing you'd want to read
good = some effective moments, uses a few techniques, has basic structure, mostly accurate. Shows potential even if inconsistent
needs_work = very brief, generic, or mostly tells rather than shows. May attempt techniques but they don't land, or structure is unclear, or SPaG significantly hinders meaning
not_valid = didn't attempt extended writing, wrote a few sentences, or is completely off-topic

passages.text: The escalator carried Sienna downward into the warm breath of the Underground — a gust of stale air and brake dust and the ghost of a thousand perfumes, all blurred into a single human scent, the smell of a city moving through its own veins. She stepped off and the platform opened before her: a curved white tunnel, tiled and bright, with a digital board that promised her train in two minutes. Two minutes. She counted the people. A woman in a green coat reading a paperback, her lips moving faintly with each line; a man in paint-spattered overalls studying nothing, his eyes fixed on the track with the glazed patience of someone who has learned to wait without thinking. The rails hummed. A draught pushed a sweet wrapper along the platform edge in small, hesitant jumps, like a mouse unsure of its direction. Then the sound came — the low, rising roar of displaced air — and the tracks began to sing, two bright lines vibrating in their cradles, and the darkness at the tunnel’s mouth shifted and thickened and became a face of metal and glass bursting into the light.
passages.label: Model A — All Skills Combined (Underground Station)

passages.text: The city softened at this hour. Leo lay on the flat roof of his grandmother’s building and watched the sky perform its nightly trick: the blue deepening through shades he had no names for — past cornflower, past ink, into a colour that felt less like a colour and more like a sound turned down. The concrete beneath his back still held the day’s warmth; it radiated upward through his T-shirt like a slow pulse, and the first stars appeared not all at once but hesitantly, the way lights come on in a building when the cleaners are working floor by floor. Below him, the street breathed out. A car alarm started and stopped. Someone laughed — a bright, carrying sound that rose six storeys and arrived cleaned of context, pure and strange. The rooftop was littered with evidence of other visits: a folding chair with a torn seat, plant pots in which nothing lived, an ashtray the rain had turned into a small grey pond. He closed his eyes. The city hummed beneath him, and the hum felt less like noise and more like a heartbeat he had always been listening to without knowing it.
passages.label: Model B — All Skills Combined (Rooftop in Summer)

passages.text: The bonfire crackled on the beach like it was alive. Halima sat close to the flames, the heat was intense on her face but her back was cold from the wind coming off the sea. Everyone was laughing and talking but she wasn’t really listening she was watching the sparks rise up into the darkness. She felt really happy and content. The sand was nice and soft under her. The fire smelled smoky which was expected. Someone was playing guitar and the music sounded beautiful like a angel singing in a church. She was absolutely over the moon about being there. The waves crashed onto the shore, they were loud and powerful and relentless and fierce and strong. Sparks drifted up like fireflies. She thought about how amazing life was and how she should appreciate moments like this one more often. The moon was as bright as a lightbulb in the sky.

passages.text: Quinn stared out of the window at the fields going past, they were green and flat and boring. She was very bored of the train journey and wanted to arrive. The man opposite was annoying because he was eating crisps loudly, the crunching sound was incredibly irritating and unbearable. She was frustrated and impatient. Outside the landscape was as flat as a pancake stretching to the horizon. The train was going really fast and everything outside was a complete blur of green and brown. She checked her phone but there was no signal which was really annoying, she sighed loudly and looked at the ceiling which was grey and uninteresting. The train smelled of crisps and coffee. It was a rubbish journey. She felt like she had been on the train for a million years and they were never going to arrive at their destination, the minutes crawled past like snails on a garden path.

passages.text: Five minutes. Esme pressed her forehead against the cool wall backstage and counted the sounds beyond the curtain: the shuffle of six hundred bodies finding their seats, the orchestra tuning in a wash of disconnected notes that hadn’t yet found their common ground, the stage manager’s radio crackling instructions she couldn’t quite hear. Four minutes. She straightened her dress — smoothed the fabric across her stomach where the nerves had knotted themselves into something physical, something with weight. Her hands trembled. She pressed them together, palm to palm, and the tremor transferred itself from one to the other like a current. Three. The house lights dimmed. She could feel it rather than see it — a shift in the air, a collective intake of breath from the auditorium that reached her through the heavy curtain as a change in pressure. Two minutes. She whispered the opening phrase: the first four bars, the rising phrase that would carry her voice out into the darkness before a single face became visible. One. The stage manager touched her shoulder. The curtain stirred. She stepped forward into the space between everything she had practised and everything she could not control.
passages.label: Countdown Narrative Model — Five Minutes Before the Concert

steps: Choose your countdown moment — the event your whole piece builds towards
Open with a Drop: start close to the moment, then pull back to build up
Use each paragraph to tighten tension — shorten sentences, increase sensory detail, slow time
Deploy your best skills: one strong simile, one semicolon contrast, one show-don't-tell moment
Reach the moment — then use a Shift or Link to end with a twist, reflection, or echo of the opening
Leave 5 minutes to proofread — upgrade one weak verb and fix any spelling or punctuation errors
method_card.title: The Countdown Narrative — Pulling It All Together
method_card.content: A countdown narrative builds towards a single moment — a door opening, a result being read, a whistle blowing. Every paragraph tightens the tension. This structure lets you showcase all your skills (vocabulary, punctuation, figurative language, show don't tell, structure) in one sustained piece.

It should include: sensory detail beyond just sight (sound, touch, temperature), precise vocabulary with strong connotations, at least one original simile or metaphor, show don't tell for any emotions, varied punctuation used for effect (at least one semicolon, dash, or short sentence for impact), and a clear structural shape (not just chronological listing). The writing should feel like a genuine creative piece — atmospheric, controlled, and purposeful. The best responses will create a clear mood and sustain it throughout.

Use everything you have learned across this unit: observation and sensory detail, precise vocabulary, punctuation for effect, show don't tell, original figurative language, and deliberate structure (Drop, Shift, Zoom, or Link). This is exam-level practice — treat it as the real thing.

gold.context: A good response weaves multiple skills together naturally rather than ticking them off as a checklist. The writing should feel like a single, unified piece of creative writing with a clear atmosphere and sense of place. At least three senses should be present. The comparison should be original and add meaning. Emotions should be implied through detail, not stated. Punctuation should be varied and purposeful. The paragraph should have a clear structural shape — perhaps narrowing focus, or building to a moment.

gold.question: This train journey passage combines every common writing mistake: comma splices, telling not showing, cliched similes, and adjective-stacking. Rewrite this section as polished, exam-quality creative writing — fix every problem and transform flat reporting into vivid, atmospheric prose.

tokens.explain: This is a comma splice — 'Halima sat close to the flames' and 'the heat was intense on her face' are both complete sentences. A comma alone cannot join them.
tokens.correction: Fix the comma splice: 'flames. The heat...' or 'flames; the heat...'

tokens.explain: 'She was absolutely over the moon about being there' tells us the emotion using a cliched idiom. This is the worst kind of telling — it names the feeling AND uses a dead phrase to do it.
tokens.correction: Show the feeling: 'She hugged her knees and watched the sparks spiral upward, each one a tiny life burning out before it reached the stars'

tokens.explain: 'Like an angel singing in a church' is a cliche — a comparison so overused it creates no image. It also contains a grammar error ('a angel' should be 'an angel').
tokens.correction: Replace with an original comparison: 'the notes drifting through the smoke like something half-remembered'

tokens.explain: Five stacked adjectives ('loud and powerful and relentless and fierce and strong') all mean roughly the same thing. Each one weakens the others. One precise verb or image is far more powerful.
tokens.correction: Replace with one strong verb: 'The waves threw themselves at the shore, dragging the shingle back with a rattling sigh'

tokens.explain: 'As bright as a lightbulb' is a weak simile — comparing the moon to something less impressive actually diminishes it. A good simile should make the reader see the thing more vividly, not less.
tokens.correction: Replace with an original comparison: 'The moon hung low and full, its light turning the wet sand to pewter'

gold.context: A good response uses the countdown structure to build tension across three stages. Each stage should foreground a different skill while maintaining consistent quality throughout. The sensory stage should engage at least two senses. The show-don't-tell stage should convey emotion through physical actions and details. The figurative language stage should include an original comparison. The final moment should feel like a threshold — the writing should stop at the edge of what happens next, leaving the reader in suspense.
gold.question: Write a short passage using the countdown structure: a character approaching a significant moment with time running out. Structure it around three numbered stages (any numbers — 'Three... Two... One...' or 'Ten minutes... Five... One...'). Each stage should use a different dominant skill: one focused on sensory detail, one on show-don't-tell emotion, and one on figurative language.

bronze.question: The countdown narrative uses different creative writing skills. Identify which skill each phrase demonstrates.

statements.text: "the nerves had knotted themselves into something physical, something with weight"
statements.explain: The writer shows anxiety through a physical sensation — a knot with weight in the stomach — rather than saying 'she was nervous.'

statements.text: "the shuffle of six hundred bodies finding their seats"
statements.explain: This is a precise auditory observation — the specific collective sound of an audience settling.

statements.text: "Her hands trembled. She pressed them together, palm to palm, and the tremor transferred itself from one to the other like a current."
statements.explain: The tremor is compared to an electrical current — an original simile that makes the physical sensation vivid.

statements.text: "Five minutes... Four minutes... Three."
statements.explain: This is the structural technique — the countdown creates urgency and momentum as time runs out.

statements.text: "the space between everything she had practised and everything she could not control"
statements.explain: The vocabulary here is precise and abstract — 'practised' vs 'could not control' captures the exact feeling of stepping on stage.

statements.text: "a wash of disconnected notes that hadn't yet found their common ground"
statements.explain: This describes the specific, recognisable sound of an orchestra tuning — a precise auditory observation.

statements.text: "the heat was intense on her face but her back was cold" (after 'Halima sat close to the flames,')"
statements.explain: Two complete sentences joined with just a comma. Needs a semicolon, full stop, or conjunction.

statements.text: "She felt really happy and content"
statements.explain: This labels two emotions directly instead of showing them through action or detail.

statements.text: "like a angel singing in a church"
statements.correct: cliche (and grammar error: should be 'an angel')
statements.explain: This simile is so familiar it creates no fresh image. It's also missing the 'n' on 'an.'

statements.text: "She was absolutely over the moon about being there"
statements.explain: 'Over the moon' is a cliched idiom, and 'absolutely over the moon' just stacks on empty intensifiers.

statements.text: "The moon was as bright as a lightbulb in the sky"
statements.explain: Comparing the moon to a lightbulb is a very common simile that actually makes the moon seem less interesting, not more.

statements.text: "She thought about how amazing life was"
statements.explain: This tells us the character's conclusion rather than showing the moment that makes her feel this way. Let the scene speak for itself.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: Audit the passage against the skills from this unit. Vocabulary: vague words like "intense", "really happy and content" (Lesson 2 problem). Punctuation: comma splice in "the heat was intense on her face but her back was cold" — two ideas that could use a semicolon for contrast (Lesson 3). Show don't tell: "She felt really happy and content" directly states the emotion (Lesson 4).

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: Fix the vocabulary first. "The heat was intense" — replace with a precise sensory detail: 'The heat pressed against her cheeks like an open oven door.' "The wind coming off the sea" — upgrade: 'the salt wind that came off the water in cold, steady gusts.' Each swap adds specificity.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: Fix the punctuation. "The heat was intense on her face but her back was cold" — this is a natural contrast, perfect for a semicolon: 'The fire pressed its heat against her cheeks; the wind laid its cold across her shoulders.' The semicolon balances the two sensations, making the contrast deliberate rather than accidental.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.content: Fix the show don't tell. Delete "She felt really happy and content" entirely. Instead, show the contentment: she lets her shoulders drop, she stops checking her phone, she tilts her head back and watches the sparks without needing to say anything. The reader should be able to name the emotion without being told it.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The fire pressed its heat against her cheeks; the salt wind laid its cold across her shoulders. Halima watched the sparks climb — a rising swarm of orange that thinned as it rose, each one winking out before it reached the stars. She let her phone slide deeper into her pocket. Around her, voices overlapped and tangled, but she wasn't following the words; she was listening to the sound of them, the rhythm of people she loved being happy, and the sound was enough. Three skills, three upgrades: precise vocabulary replaces vague words, a semicolon balances the fire/wind contrast, and the emotion is shown through action (letting the phone slide away, listening without needing to speak) rather than told.

worked_examples.passage: The bonfire crackled on the beach like it was alive. Halima sat close to the flames, the heat was intense on her face but her back was cold from the wind coming off the sea. Everyone was laughing and talking but she wasn’t really listening she was watching the sparks rise up into the darkness. She felt really happy and content.
worked_examples.question: How does this weak passage fail to use the skills covered in this unit, and how would you improve it?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: Identify the structural choice. "Five minutes." This is a countdown narrative (Lesson 6) — the whole piece builds towards a single moment. The two-word opening is also a Drop: no introduction, no backstory, just a ticking clock. The reader immediately feels the pressure of time.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: Find the show don't tell. Esme "pressed her forehead against the cool wall" — this single action tells us she's nervous, seeking comfort from the cold surface, grounding herself. She doesn't say 'I'm terrified.' She just presses her head against a wall, and we understand.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: Examine the punctuation at work. The colon after "counted the sounds beyond the curtain" opens a list — a deliberate slowing-down as Esme breaks the overwhelming noise into individual parts. This is what anxious people do: they try to control chaos by itemising it. The punctuation mirrors the psychology.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.content: Look at the vocabulary precision. "A wash of disconnected notes that hadn't yet found their common ground" does double duty — literally the orchestra is tuning, but the phrase also describes Esme's state: she hasn't found her own ground yet either. Notice how every skill serves the scene rather than competing for attention. There isn't a simile in every sentence. The punctuation varies but doesn't show off. This is what mastery looks like: all the skills running together, none of them demanding attention for themselves.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: This passage demonstrates all five skills working in harmony. Structure: the countdown narrative ('Five minutes') creates immediate tension. Show don't tell: forehead against the wall conveys anxiety through action. Punctuation: the colon opens a controlled list that mirrors the character's attempt to manage her fear. Vocabulary: 'disconnected notes that hadn't yet found their common ground' describes both the orchestra and Esme's own unreadiness. Figurative language is deliberately restrained — the writing trusts sensory detail over simile. In your own exam writing, aim for this integration: each skill should serve the scene, not advertise itself. One strong structural choice, one show-don't-tell action, one precise vocabulary decision, one well-placed punctuation mark — deployed together, they create writing that reads as confident and controlled.

worked_examples.passage: Five minutes. Esme pressed her forehead against the cool wall backstage and counted the sounds beyond the curtain: the shuffle of six hundred bodies finding their seats, the orchestra tuning in a wash of disconnected notes that hadn’t yet found their common ground, the stage manager’s radio crackling instructions she couldn’t quite hear.

ai_marking_prompts.creative_writing:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor giving formative feedback on a student's short creative writing (around 80-120 words). This is a practice task — your goal is to encourage and develop.

Assess whether the student:
1. Created a clear ATMOSPHERE or MOOD through their writing choices
2. Used SPECIFIC detail rather than vague generalisations
3. Showed some CRAFT — deliberate vocabulary choices, varied sentences, or figurative language
4. Engaged the reader — does the writing create a picture or feeling?

IMPORTANT: This is short creative writing, not an essay. Reward imagination and voice. A student who writes vividly about a simple scene is doing better than one who uses forced figurative language on every line. Quality over quantity. Be genuinely encouraging — creative writing is personal and students need confidence.

Respond in JSON:
{"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences","improvement":"optional suggestion"}

excellent = vivid, engaging writing with clear atmosphere, specific detail, and deliberate craft. Shows a genuine writer's voice
good = creates some atmosphere or imagery, uses some specific detail, shows effort with vocabulary or technique even if inconsistent
needs_work = very generic or vague, mostly tells rather than shows, little evidence of deliberate craft
not_valid = didn't attempt creative writing, wrote a single sentence, or is completely off-topic
ai_marking_prompts.improve_sentence:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor giving formative feedback on a student's rewritten sentence. The student was shown a weak sentence and asked to improve it by upgrading vocabulary, sentence structure, or technique.

Assess whether the student:
1. Made a genuine IMPROVEMENT — is the rewrite better than the original?
2. Addressed the specific weakness (vague vocabulary, telling not showing, flat structure, clichéd language)
3. Maintained the original MEANING while improving the quality

IMPORTANT: There are many valid ways to improve a sentence. Do NOT penalise creative choices. If the student's version is more vivid, precise, or engaging than the original, that counts as improvement even if it's different from what you'd write. Be encouraging.

Respond in JSON:
{"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences","improvement":"optional suggestion"}

excellent = significantly better than the original, shows flair or originality, addresses the weakness effectively
good = clearly improved on the original, addresses the main weakness even if it could go further
needs_work = barely changed, or changed something but not the main weakness, or introduced new problems
not_valid = didn't attempt a rewrite, or made the sentence worse
ai_marking_prompts.creative_writing_extended:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor giving formative feedback on a student's extended creative writing (around 150-200+ words). This simulates the Paper 1 Q5 creative writing task worth up to 40 marks.

Assess whether the student:
1. Created a sustained ATMOSPHERE or MOOD — not just one good sentence but a consistent feel throughout
2. Used a range of TECHNIQUES — sensory language, figurative language, varied sentence structures, effective punctuation
3. Showed STRUCTURAL awareness — the piece has shape (a beginning that hooks, development, and an ending that resonates)
4. Demonstrated TECHNICAL ACCURACY — spelling, punctuation, and grammar that support rather than hinder the writing
5. Has a VOICE — the writing sounds like it belongs to someone, not like a template

IMPORTANT: This is formative practice. Reward ambition even when execution is imperfect. A student who attempts a complex structure and partly succeeds is showing more skill than one who plays it safe. Be encouraging but specific about what would strengthen the piece.

Respond in JSON:
{"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"3-4 sentences","improvement":"specific suggestion"}

excellent = sustained atmosphere, range of techniques used effectively, clear structure, accurate SPaG, distinctive voice. This is writing you'd want to read
good = some effective moments, uses a few techniques, has basic structure, mostly accurate. Shows potential even if inconsistent
needs_work = very brief, generic, or mostly tells rather than shows. May attempt techniques but they don't land, or structure is unclear, or SPaG significantly hinders meaning
not_valid = didn't attempt extended writing, wrote a few sentences, or is completely off-topic
